slides.title: Where we are
items: Nothing from Tuesday is a prerequisite for today. No EXTI, no NVIC, no ISR, no volatile — this is a new peripheral and a new protocol.
Two habits carry over: go to the reference manual for a number rather than guessing it, and assign a whole mask to a control register rather than compound-assigning one bit into it.
The first half of the hour is looking rather than building: wire a display to two pins, flash five lines of given code, and put the oscilloscope on the wires.
The second half is the peripheral that produced what you saw.
slides.presenterNote: ≈ 2 min with announcements. Say the pivot out loud — several students will assume Tuesday is required.

Recap
items: Two wires, shared by everything on them: a clock the controller drives, and a data line every device can pull LOW and none can drive HIGH.
A transaction is START, seven address bits, the R/W bit, an ACK from whoever recognized the address, data bytes each with their own ACK, and a STOP. You have one on a screen with your name on it.
A library needs five operations: initialize, one byte out, one byte in, several bytes out, several bytes in — and the multi-byte pair carry an address inside the device.
One assignment to I2C_CR2 describes an entire transaction. The peripheral does the rest; nothing in the library counts a clock edge.
PRESC is f_I2CCLK / 4 MHz − 1, which is why there is no 12 MHz row and we did not need one.
What you #define is always the 7-bit address. The library shifts it.
No new homework tonight — Tuesday's timer program is what is due. Leave the display wired: Thursday is the chip at the other end of these two wires.
